1.1: 1.1 Argument. The Apostle writes the second Epistle to the Thessalonians, and makes known to them about the last times and the casting down of the adversary. He writes this Epistle from Athens through Titus the deacon and Onesimus the acolyte.
1.3: 1.3 To give thanks, etc. Here he gives thanks to God for their goods, lest perhaps they be puffed up over the so great good which they had from God, as though having it from themselves. One toward another. So that, namely, he who is loved may love others, and by mutual services show charity.
1.5: 1.5 For an example of the just, etc. For if he punishes sins so severely in the penitent, what will he do to the hardened? He says this so that it may be understood that he who does not spare the just will not spare the impious. Just: if indeed it is just, which is established as being so. For if indeed is not put here for doubt but for affirmation, hence another translator says: Since he is just, etc.
1.7: 1.7 At the revelation. He begins to show how horrible the tribulation will be for those, and how pleasant the rest for these.
1.8: 1.8 Of the Lord Jesus. Coming in a flame of fire, not that he is surrounded by flame, but in effect, because he will burn up his enemies. To them that know not God. For there are others who do not know the law.
1.9: 1.9 Who shall suffer punishment. That is, will endure. For to give is sometimes put for to endure, so here also. And fittingly, for he who suffers gives to him whom he has offended punishments, as it were welcome. In eternal destruction. As if he said: They will always feel the punishments, yet will not always fail. When he shall come to be glorified, etc. For he will be seen bright and wonderful in the believers, but will appear severe to the unbelievers, when he will confine them in eternal punishments. And the brief sense of these words is: He will come to punish the wicked and glorify the good.
1.10: 1.10 Because our testimony. Therefore he gives you who are afflicted rest with us, because the testimony, that is, whatever we said about that day of judgment, you believed, about the glory of the good and the punishment of the wicked.
1.11: 1.11 Wherefore. The order of the words is this: On which day we pray that he may deign, that is, judge you worthy: We always pray. Or in which, that is, for which, or in avoiding the danger of which day, we must always pray. The work of faith. That is, the confession which is properly the work of faith in virtue, so that they can in no way be turned from confession. Or, the work of faith, every good which faith demands, and without which faith is dead. In power of perseverance, that is, that he may give you perseverance to the end.
2.1: 2.1 And we beseech you, brethren, by the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, etc. Up to this point he said that he gives thanks for them and prays; here he determines about the day of judgment, beseeching them not to receive lightly and easily an opinion about the coming of the Lord as though imminent, or to be frightened.
2.2: 2.2 That you be not soon moved. As if he said: If you are moved, it is quickly; for nothing is brought on you that lasts long. Nor by spirit. That is, if a malign spirit, appearing as an angel of light in a vision, persuade you of this. Or, if anyone says that through the Holy Spirit revealing it he has learned that the day of judgment is at hand, do not believe. Nor by epistle. For deceivers are accustomed, in order to deceive, to forge an epistle under the name of some famous man, so that the authority of the name may commend what by itself could not be received. As if the day of the Lord were at hand. He does not say this in such a way as not to wish them to have their loins girded and lamps burning in their hands, waiting for the Lord to return from the wedding.
2.4: 2.4 In the temple. Or, the temple. Some want not only the prince himself to be understood in this place but his whole body, that is, the multitude of men belonging to him together with the prince himself; and they think it more correct to say, as it is in the Greek, not in the temple but into the temple of God he sits, as if he with his own were the temple of God, which is the Church. As it is said: He sits into a friend, that is, as a friend.
2.5: 2.5 Because unless there come. He speaks secretly of the destruction of the Roman empire, lest he provoke them to persecute the Church. Or he says this of the spiritual rule of the Roman Church, or of a departure from the faith. Unless the apostate come first. So some codices have. That he said this of Antichrist, whom he calls apostate, no one doubts: certainly from the Lord God. For if this can rightly be said of all the impious, how much more of him! The son of perdition. Antichrist, not by nature but by imitation.
2.6: 2.6 You know. He says that they know what restrains, and does not expose it openly, and so we do not know, except that some suspect it was said of the Roman empire, until it be taken away, or be made out of the midst. And that the Apostle did not wish to write it openly, lest he incur the calumny of having ill-wished the Roman empire, since it was hoped to be eternal. In his time. When the accession to the Roman empire and to obedience of the Roman Church is complete, there will be a departure from both empires; when this is fulfilled, that wicked one will be present, the time of mercy being fulfilled in which the fullness of the Gentiles enters into the faith: the departure will be revealed, and so the day of the Lord will be at hand.
2.7: 2.7 For the mystery, etc. Already in the very beginnings of the accession iniquity is found, but mystical, that is, cloaked under the name of piety, so that they wish to be held as ministers of Christ while they are false. The devil secretly through Nero and others killed martyrs, as through that one he is then going to do openly, killing Elijah and Enoch and very many others; and Nero and the others are a shadow of the future Antichrist, as David and Abel of Christ. Until he be taken out of the way. That is, until that power of the Roman empire is taken from the midst of the world, because all from everywhere flowed together to Rome as to the head. Or, let him who holds the faith hold it until it itself grows cold. Or, let him who restrains him, that is, the accession to the faith, restrain, until it itself be taken from the midst. Or, until iniquity, which is now mystical, be made out of the midst, that is, as of common things, so that a man is not ashamed to commit adultery or to steal, any more than to walk or to speak. Be made out of the midst. Namely the departure, that is, let it appear manifestly; and then, the departure from the true God now revealed, charity now grown cold from the abundance of iniquity, he will be revealed, etc.
2.8: 2.8 With the spirit of his mouth. That is, by the power of the Holy Spirit, who is called the spirit of the mouth, because he proceeds from him.
2.9: 2.9 In lying wonders and in all seduction. Those signs are called lies, either because they will not be true as they seem, but fantastic; or if true, by God's permission they will draw to a lie. Therefore God shall send them. AUGUSTINE, book 20 of the City of God, chapter 19. God will permit the devil to do these things, etc., up to: others most unjustly judged.
2.13: 2.13 The firstfruits unto salvation. That is, that we should believe in Christ and confess the faith not in that dangerous last time but in the primitive Church. Or, we apostles are the firstfruits of all believers, because the apostles believed first, and this for the salvation of all nations.
2.14: 2.14 To the purchasing of the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ. Or, that you may be a possession in which God is glorified.
2.16: 2.16 And has given us consolation. By promising the kingdom of heaven. In grace. That is, through the grace which he gave we hope for eternal things. Or he gave all these not for our merit but in his grace.
3.1: 3.1 For the rest, brethren, pray. He exhorts that we must pray that God may deign to direct his teaching in an unwearied course and pour it through the mouths of the apostles into the ears of the hearers, and from the ears into the hearts, that the seditions of the wicked may be restrained.
3.2: 3.2 That we may be delivered. From false apostles, lest they seduce our people, or lay snares for us. Or, that we may be delivered from importunate men, that is, unbelievers who resist the word of God and do not stand in the harbor of quiet. And from evil men, who persecute the faithful. I say deliver us because not all have yet received the faith through me who are to receive it. For all men have not faith. That is, not all are going to believe even if you pray, but only those preordained to the adoption of sons.
3.6: 3.6 We declare to you. He begins about the busybodies and the idle, admonishing the good to correct them.
3.7: 3.7 You yourselves know how you ought to imitate us. And since those do not do these things, you must avoid them. Or, they walk not according to the tradition. For you know how I conducted myself, which you do not see in them; as if he said: There is no need for me to explain to you that tradition, because you know it, that we were not restless, like those who care for others' affairs, wandering hither and thither.
3.9: 3.9 But that we might give ourselves. It should be noted that the Apostle not only taught by words but exhorted also by deeds. For it belongs to a fit teacher to fulfil in works what he teaches in words.
3.10: 3.10 For if any man will not work. Some say that the Apostle commanded this about spiritual works; otherwise, if he said it about bodily work, in which farmers or craftsmen labor, he would seem to think contrary to the Lord, who says in the Gospel: Be not solicitous what you shall eat (Matthew 6), etc. But they strive needlessly to draw darkness over themselves and others, so that what charity usefully admonishes they not only do not want to do but do not even want to understand, when in many other places of the epistles the Apostle teaches most openly what he means here. For he wishes the servants of God to work bodily, to have the means of living, so that they are not compelled by want to ask for necessaries. Nor is it against what was said before: Be not solicitous what you shall eat, etc. For this was not said so that they should not provide as much as suffices for necessity, from where they could honorably, but that they should not look to these things, nor do for their sake whatever they are commanded to do for the preaching of the Gospel.
3.11: 3.11 Doing nothing but meddling. This deed is abhorrent to the Lord's discipline, for their god is the belly, who with a foul care provide necessaries for themselves.
3.13: 3.13 Be not weary. Because even if they work, they may nevertheless need something. And therefore he warns that those who had the means of supplying necessaries to the servants of God should not grow slack on this occasion. For he who is kind in giving does not come under reproach; but this one does, who, when he can bear labor, wishes to live in idleness.
